mcqs.question: What is the greedy-choice property, and how does it differ from optimal substructure?
options: The greedy-choice property guarantees that the locally best choice at each step is always part of some globally optimal solution and never needs revisiting — optimal substructure only says the best overall answer is built from best answers to smaller subproblems, without saying which choice is safe to lock in
They are the same requirement, just named differently across algorithm texts
The greedy-choice property applies to DP problems; optimal substructure applies only to greedy ones
The greedy-choice property is only relevant to problems involving sorting
mcqs.explanation: Optimal substructure alone (shared with DP) doesn't tell you a single locally-best choice is always safe — that extra, stronger guarantee is exactly the greedy-choice property, and it's the part that must be separately proven, usually via an exchange argument.

mcqs.question: With coin denominations {1, 3, 4}, why does 'always take the largest coin that fits' fail to make change for 6 optimally?
options: It doesn't fail — 4+1+1 is in fact optimal for this denomination set
Taking the 4 first forecloses the 3+3 solution, which uses fewer coins, and greedy never reconsiders a coin once taken
The algorithm produces an invalid amount, not just a suboptimal one
Greedy fails only because the denominations aren't sorted first
mcqs.explanation: Greedy commits to the 4 immediately because it's locally largest, but that choice removes any path to the 2-coin answer (3+3) — greedy never backtracks to reconsider, which is exactly the property that makes it fail here despite giving a valid (just non-optimal) answer.

mcqs.question: An interval-scheduling problem could plausibly be sorted by start time, finish time, or duration. What's the risk of picking one without justification?
options: There's no risk — any consistent sort order produces the same greedy result for interval problems
The code will fail to compile if the wrong key is chosen
Sorting always requires O(n log n) regardless of key, so the choice doesn't matter for correctness or performance

Only one of the plausible sort keys may actually be safe (i.e., have a valid exchange argument); the others can produce code that runs and looks reasonable while giving wrong answers on untested inputs
mcqs.explanation: Multiple sort keys often look equally plausible, but typically only one has an actual proof of safety behind it (as activity-selection's finish-time key does) — an unjustified choice can silently produce wrong answers on inputs that weren't part of casual testing, without any error or crash to signal the problem.

mcqs.question: Why does a wrong greedy algorithm often pass the small examples a candidate tests by hand?
options: Small examples are usually chosen for being easy to trace by hand, not for being adversarial, so they rarely happen to hit the specific input shape that exposes the greedy's flaw
Small examples always test every edge case by definition
Wrong greedy algorithms are mathematically guaranteed to work on inputs of size 3 or fewer
It's actually rare for a wrong greedy to pass small examples — most fail immediately
mcqs.explanation: Hand-picked test examples are chosen for tractability, not adversarial coverage, so a greedy flaw that only surfaces on a specific input shape (like {1,3,4} targeting 6) is easy to miss entirely unless you deliberately try to construct a breaking case.
